notes: Owner math, first run: Friday 2026-10-16 (posted on demand the day the pipeline went live), then every weekday from 2026-10-19 to 2026-11-12 (7 AM). From 2026-10-21 the 6 PM slot and the weekend mornings are added here in (date, slot) order: feature Reels of the demo app, tips and myth vs fact (the rotation in scripts/schedule.mjs); November's own posts are in 2026-11.json. The first run's cards and videos stay as rendered; from October 20 their captions lead with a search keyword and carry five hashtags from brand.json's pools (scripts/hashtags.mjs). Themes: the rendered posts keep theirs; new posts take the theme that differs from their neighbors. Every figure is recomputed by scripts/verify.mjs from scripts/compute.mjs; rules of thumb are labeled as such.

posts.hook: What is one labor point actually worth?

result.label: One labor point, per store, per year

posts.takeaway: Across 10 stores: $160,000 a year. Two scheduled hours a day per store is the whole point.
posts.caption:
Labor cost math for restaurant and coffee shop owners: what one labor point is worth at a $1,600,000 store.
1% of $1,600,000 = $16,000 a year per store.
That is $43.84 a day, or 2.2 hours at $20 an hour.
Across 10 stores, one labor point is $160,000.

posts.hook: Is 29.3% labor good or bad?

steps.label: Net sales this week, not gross

posts.takeaway: Track it weekly per store on net sales; here one point is $328 a week.
posts.caption:
Labor cost percentage for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: how to calculate it and what it means.
Wages $9,610 ÷ net sales $32,800 = 29.3% labor.
One labor point at this store is $328 a week.
Net sales, not gross, is the bottom of the fraction.

posts.hook: Your labor number is missing 7.65%.
posts.takeaway: Compare targets on loaded labor: the 7.65% is Social Security and Medicare; benefits add more.
posts.caption:
Fully loaded labor cost for small business owners: adding employer payroll tax to wages.
Wages $9,600 + 7.65% employer payroll tax = $10,334.40.
On $32,800 of net sales that is 31.5% labor, not 29.3%.
Benefits and workers' comp come on top.

posts.hook: How much does one labor hour sell?
posts.takeaway: Labor % is wage ÷ SPLH: $18.46 ÷ $63.08 = 29.3%. Schedule to an SPLH floor.
posts.caption:
Sales per labor hour (SPLH) for restaurant, coffee shop and franchise owners: the fairest way to compare stores.
$32,800 of net sales ÷ 520 hours worked = $63.08 per labor hour.
Average wage $18.46 ÷ $63.08 = 29.3% labor.
SPLH compares stores fairly even when wages differ.

Labor % turns amber or red when a store runs over its own target.

posts.hook: Ten overtime hours. $322.95. Here's the math.
posts.formula: Hours × wage × 1.5, plus employer payroll tax

result.label: What those 10 hours cost, fully loaded

posts.takeaway: The premium alone is $5,597.80 a year if it repeats weekly. Flag anyone past 32 hours by Thursday.
posts.caption:
Overtime cost for restaurant, salon and coffee shop owners: what 10 overtime hours really cost.
10 overtime hours × $20 × 1.5 = $300, or $322.95 with 7.65% employer tax.
The same hours at straight time cost $215.30. The premium is $107.65 a week.
Every week for a year: $5,597.80 from one person.

posts.hook: Do your stores share one bank account?
posts.title: Separate bank accounts
lines: Give every store's LLC its own operating account.
Each store's deposits land in its own account.
Pay shared costs from one, bill back in writing.
Mixed accounts turn month-end into a sorting job.
posts.takeaway: Clean bank lines make every month-end shorter, for you and your bookkeeper.
posts.caption:
One bank account per LLC: a bookkeeping tip for multi-store franchise, restaurant and salon owners.
Give each store's LLC its own operating account, and let its deposits land there.
Pay shared costs from one account and bill the others back in writing.
Mixed accounts turn every month-end into a sorting job.
How many of your stores share an account?

posts.hook: Food cost 28%? Your COGS is 31.5%.

result.label: COGS %, the number to price on

posts.takeaway: Price and target on COGS, not food cost: 3.5 points is $4,900 a month in cups and bags.
posts.caption:
Food cost vs COGS for restaurant and coffee shop owners: why paper and packaging count.
Food $39,200 ÷ net sales $140,000 = 28.0% food cost.
Add $4,900 of paper and packaging: COGS is $44,100, or 31.5%.
Price and set targets on COGS.

claims.text: Each store's page shows its sales and labor % day by day with the target line, and the store's P&L
A store P&L shows net income only when every month in view is complete; otherwise it says so

posts.caption:
Daily labor cost by store for restaurant and franchise owners: see which days ran over target.
Store 106 in Rhea's demo company runs high labor on purpose, in sample data.
Each day: net sales from the POS and labor % from the time clock, against the store's target line.

posts.hook: Labor % on gross sales flatters every store.
posts.title: Divide by net sales
lines: Gross sales include discounts you never collected.
Register totals include sales tax and tips.
Net sales is what the stores actually earned.
Use the same denominator at every store.
posts.takeaway: Same wages, different denominator, different story. Make every store's labor % use net sales.
posts.caption:
Net sales vs gross sales: which one restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners should divide by.
Gross sales include discounts and comps you never collected.
Register totals also hold sales tax and tips, which aren't yours.
Labor %, food cost and prime cost all divide by net sales, at every store.

posts.hook: If there's money in the bank, we're profitable.
why: Sales tax and tips sit in that balance.
Gift card money is still owed to guests.
This month's bills and payroll clear later.
posts.takeaway: Profit is on the P&L. The bank balance is a timing question.
posts.caption:
Cash vs profit for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: why the bank balance isn't what you made.
The bank balance holds money that isn't yours yet: sales tax, tips, gift card balances.
Bills and payroll for the same month often clear later.
Profit is on the P&L; the bank shows timing.
Who on your team reads the bank balance as profit?

posts.hook: 63.5¢ of every dollar is gone before rent.
posts.takeaway: Rule of thumb: prime cost under 60%. These 3.5 points are $4,900 a month, every month.
posts.caption:
Prime cost for restaurant owners and franchise operators: food plus labor as a share of sales.
COGS $44,100 + fully loaded labor $44,800 = $88,900 prime cost.
On $140,000 of net sales that is 63.5%.
Rule of thumb: keep it under 60%. The gap here is $4,900 a month.

Names and hours from the time clock, never pay, so a manager can trim a shift in time.

posts.keyword: rent as a percentage of sales
posts.hook: Rent is fixed. Rent % isn't.
posts.takeaway: Rule of thumb: occupancy under 10% of sales. Below $119,000 a month this lease breaks it.
posts.caption:
Rent as a percentage of sales for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: occupancy cost explained.
Rent and CAM $11,900 ÷ net sales $140,000 = 8.5%.
The same rent on a $100,000 month is 11.9%.
Rule of thumb: keep occupancy under 10%. That line sits at $119,000 a month here.

posts.hook: Can you compare your stores line by line?
posts.title: One chart of accounts
lines: Every store's books use the same account list.
Same names, same numbers, same order.
Then any line compares across stores.
Add an account once, for every store.
posts.takeaway: When one store says Supplies and another says Paper goods, nobody can compare them.
posts.caption:
Chart of accounts tip for multi-store owners: use the same accounts at every store and LLC.
Give every store and LLC the same account names, numbers and order.
Then food cost, labor and rent compare across stores line by line.
When one store says Supplies and another says Paper goods, nobody can.

posts.hook: 8% off the top is $115,200 a year.
posts.takeaway: Fees are figured on sales before any cost. Budget labor and COGS on the 92% you keep.
posts.caption:
Franchise royalty and ad fund math for multi-unit owners: what 8% of sales takes from a month.
6% royalty + 2% ad fund on a $120,000 month = $9,600.
That is $320 a day, and $115,200 over twelve months like this.
Franchise fees come off sales before any cost.

Sales and discounts, sales tax owed, tips owed to staff, card sales waiting to be paid out, cash.
Debits equal credits, every day, every store.

posts.hook: Your store starts earning on the 22nd.
posts.takeaway: Know each store's break-even day. After it, 38¢ of every dollar is profit.
posts.caption:
Break-even point for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: the sales per day where a store starts earning.
Fixed costs $38,500 ÷ 38% contribution margin = $101,316 a month to break even.
That is $3,377 a day. At $4,667 a day, the store breaks even on day 22.
After that, 38¢ of every sales dollar is profit.

posts.hook: One P&L for the whole group is enough.
posts.fact: Every store needs its own P&L.
why: A strong store can cover a weak one.
Rent, labor and sales differ by location.
posts.takeaway: Read the group total, then every store's month beside it.
posts.caption:
Store-level P&L for multi-store owners: why one group P&L hides the store that loses money.
A group P&L adds the strong stores and the weak ones together.
One store losing money every month can hide inside a profitable total.
Read each store's P&L beside the others, same month, same accounts.

posts.hook: $8,250 of your deposits aren't yours.
posts.formula: Register totals ÷ (1 + tax rate) = net sales

steps.label: Owed to the state per day (÷ 30)

posts.takeaway: Book tax to a liability the day it's collected; the deposit looks 8.25% bigger than your sales.
posts.caption:
Sales tax bookkeeping for small business owners: why collected tax is a liability, not revenue.
$108,250 rang through the registers at 8.25% tax.
Net sales are $100,000; the other $8,250 belongs to the state.
Book it as a liability on the day, not as sales.

why: A missing deposit is easy to find in weeks.
Twelve months later, nobody remembers why.
Monthly numbers let you act this year.
posts.takeaway: Books closed monthly answer questions while they still matter.

Monthly bookkeeping for small business owners: why catching up at year-end is the slow way.
A year-end catch-up finds problems after the year is over.
A missing deposit or a wrong bill is easy to trace within weeks, hard after months.
Close every month, and the numbers are useful while you can still act.

By then the hours are spent.

Compare each store with its own target.

posts.caption:
Labor cost percentage, daily: why restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners shouldn't wait for payroll.
Payroll arrives days after the shifts, when the hours are already spent.
Each morning, read yesterday's labor % for every store against its own target.
A daily look turns a payroll surprise into a one-shift fix.
When do you see labor % today?

posts.hook: A $9,000 tip month costs you $922.50.
posts.formula: Tips in = tips out; only tax and fees are yours

steps.label: As sales they'd overstate sales by

posts.takeaway: Tips go to a payable account the day they're collected; only the taxes and fees hit your P&L.
posts.caption:
Tip accounting for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: tips are a payable, not sales.
$9,000 in card tips is $0 of revenue: it is owed to the team.
What it costs you: 7.65% employer tax ($688.50) and the 2.6% card fee ($234.00), before any FICA tip credit.
That is $922.50 to pass $9,000 through. The FICA tip credit (Form 8846) may cut it: ask your CPA whether you qualify.

posts.hook: $14,000 of gift cards sold isn't sales.

steps.label: Sold in December: not sales yet
Redeemed in December: this is sales

posts.takeaway: Still owed after January: $4,700. December looks rich and January poor unless the liability is booked.
posts.caption:
Gift card accounting for coffee shop, salon and restaurant owners: a liability until redeemed.
$14,000 of gift cards sold in December, $3,100 redeemed.
On December 31 you owe gift card holders $10,900; after January's $6,200, still $4,700.
Sales happen when the card is used, not when it is sold.

posts.hook: Your 2.6% card rate is really 3.1%.
posts.formula: (Rate × card sales + fee × transactions) ÷ card sales
posts.takeaway: Small tickets make the 10¢ matter: check the effective rate on the statement, not the quoted one.
posts.caption:
Credit card processing fees for small business owners: the effective rate on small tickets.
2.6% of $40,000 = $1,040, plus 10¢ × 1,900 transactions = $190.
$1,230 in fees on $40,000 is an effective rate of 3.1%.
At a $21.05 average ticket, the dime is 15.4% of the fee.

posts.hook: 0.6% sounds small. It's $43,200.
posts.takeaway: Across 12 stores: $43,200 a year. Pull each statement's effective rate quarterly and negotiate on group volume.
posts.caption:
Card processing rates for multi-unit restaurant and franchise owners: 2.9% vs 2.3% on $600,000 a year.
2.9% of $600,000 = $17,400. 2.3% = $13,800.
Six tenths of a point is $3,600 per store per year, $300 a month.
Across 12 stores: $43,200.

posts.hook: Where is Saturday's money on Sunday night?
posts.formula: Card sales per day × days until funding

steps.label: Fri, Sat and Sun all fund on Monday

result.label: In transit on Sunday night, per store

posts.takeaway: Across 12 stores that's $136,800 not yet in the bank. Reconcile card sales to payouts by day.
posts.caption:
Card settlement timing for restaurant and franchise owners: weekend sales reach the bank on Monday.
With next-business-day funding, Friday, Saturday and Sunday card sales all land on Monday (Tuesday after a holiday).
At $3,800 a day that is $11,400 in transit on Sunday night, per store; $136,800 across 12.
Averaged over the week, every card sale waits 1.4 days.

posts.hook: One missing deposit = $28,750 of sales.
posts.formula: Loss ÷ net margin = sales to earn it back
posts.takeaway: Match every deposit to its sales day within the week, while the drawer and the shift are fresh.
posts.caption:
Missing deposit math for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: what one lost deposit costs.
A $2,875 deposit that shows up 30 days late costs $21.27 of interest at 9%.
One that never shows up costs $2,875, which at a 10% margin takes $28,750 of sales to earn back.
Match deposits to sales days every week.

posts.hook: Short $75.60 a month: normal or a problem?
posts.takeaway: Rule of thumb: under 0.3%, drifting both ways, is counting. The same shift always short is a conversation.
posts.caption:
Cash over and short for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: how much drawer variance is normal.
Cash sales 18% × $140,000 = $25,200 a month, $840 a day.
0.3% of that is $2.52 a day, $75.60 a month.
Rule of thumb: that much, drifting over and short, is counting noise. One shift always short is not.

posts.hook: Fifty cents a ticket is $69,350 a year.

result.label: A year of 50¢ more per ticket

posts.takeaway: Ticket size moves with a question at the register; traffic needs a marketing budget. Start cheap.
posts.caption:
Average ticket and transaction count for restaurant, coffee shop and salon owners: the cheaper sales lever.
$12.40 × 380 transactions = $4,712 a day.
50¢ more per ticket adds $190 a day; 15 more transactions add $186.
The 50¢ is $69,350 a year, and it costs a question at the register.

posts.hook: One labor point is 4% more profit.

result.label: More profit, from one labor point

posts.takeaway: At a 24.8% margin, one labor point moves profit 4%. Watch labor weekly, not when the P&L lands.
posts.caption:
Four-wall profit for franchise and multi-unit restaurant owners: what one labor point adds.
$1,400,000 × 24.8% = $347,200 of four-wall profit.
One labor point is $14,000, taking profit to $361,200: 4.0% more.
At this margin, profit moves about four times faster than labor.
